Your body goes still, you can’t feel much but, at the same time, your senses are working overtime.
You know you must act soon, but it’s as if something is stopping you.
This “freezing”, or tonic immobility in academic terms, is an adaptive defense response to stress or danger.
While fight-or-flight seems logical for survival, freezing appears counterproductive – potentially too much to handle, making us incapable of acting or making a decision.

When I first started traveling, my dad asked me what I was running away from.
Another time, a friend told me to stop running away from my problems and to start living life.
I’m running away because I want to experience every culture, see every mountain, eat different food, attend crazy festivals, meet new people, and enjoy different holidays around the world.
In our society, the accepted path is long and narrow: you go to college, get a job, get married, buy a house, have two or three children, raise them, and then retire.
Only then, after you’ve put in your time, can you enjoy the fruits of your labor.
For me, those who travel the world aren’t running away from life.
They have a degree of freedom a lot of people will never experience.
They get to be the captains of their own ships.
I am just going after my own life.
And I never plan to look back.
On the contrary, they are running toward true living.
